slides.title: Wi-Fi Architecture
slides.body:
The Building Block – BSS
Basic Service Set (BSS) is the basic unit of a wireless network, consisting of one Access Point (AP) and its connected devices.
AP acts as the central communication point
Devices communicate through the AP
AP connects devices to the LAN or internet
BSSID is the AP’s MAC address
BSA is the AP’s coverage area

slides.body:
SSID (Service Set Identifier)
Human-readable, case-sensitive name (up to 32 characters) of a Wi-Fi network, used to distinguish between networks
 It can be modified, and devices connect using the SSID. The BSSID (MAC address of the AP) is not visible to users

Analogy
Analogy: Think of the AP as a classroom teacher. All students (devices) communicate through the teacher (AP). Students do not talk directly to each other during class — they raise their hand, the teacher acknowledges, then the communication happens. This is how all data flows in a BSS.

slides.title: Ad-Hoc Mode
slides.body:
IBSS – Independent BSS
Peer-to-Peer: Devices connect directly without an Access Point (AP)
Limited Range: No internet unless shared by a device
Modern Use: Rare today, but used in some IoT devices
Example: Two laptops directly communicating without an AP (traditional IBSS)

slides.title: Ad-Hoc Mode
slides.body:
Analogy
Ad-Hoc mode is like a small group of friends talking directly to each other
There’s no teacher or coordinator, so everyone communicates peer-to-peer
Communication works only within the group and stops if someone leaves,  unlike ESS

slides.title: 1. WEP
slides.body:
Why WEP is Broken:
WEP uses a short 24-bit IV, so IVs repeat quickly in heavy traffic
Repeated IVs allow attackers to compare packets and derive the key
Tools like Aircrack-ng can crack WEP within minutes
WEP was deprecated by IEEE in 2004 and should not be used

slides.title: 2. WPA
slides.body:
A Transition from WEP
Content:
WPA, introduced in 2003 as a temporary replacement for WEP until WPA2 was ready, was based on the IEEE 802.11i draft. 
It used TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) for better security, generating a new 128-bit key per packet and replacing WEP’s CRC with a Message Integrity Check (MIC). 
While it improved security, flaws in the Michael algorithm were later discovered, exposing vulnerabilities.
WPA was introduced in 2003 as a temporary replacement for WEP until WPA2 was ready
It was based on the IEEE 802.11i draft and used TKIP for better security
TKIP generated a new 128-bit key per packet and replaced WEP’s CRC with MIC for message integrity
However, flaws were later found in the Michael algorithm, making WPA vulnerable

slides.title: 2. WPA
slides.body:
Key Points
WPA replaces WEP with better encryption and data integrity
It laid the foundation for WPA2, which was a more secure solution

slides.body:
Introduction
Key Features of WPA2
Uses AES-CCMP (Advanced Encryption Standard – Counter Mode with CBC-MAC Protocol)
Stronger encryption than WEP and WPA
Two modes of operation:
WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2), introduced in 2004, replaced WEP and WPA, using AES encryption (the same used by banks and governments) to ensure strong security

slides.title: WPA2-Personal
slides.body:
WPA2-PSK
Most commonly used for home Wi-Fi networks
Uses a Pre-Shared Key (password) that is the same for all users
Easy to set up but less secure than WPA2-Enterprise

slides.title: 3. WPA2
slides.body:
WPA2-Enterprise:
Used in business or institutional networks, 
It uses EAP with a central server like RADIUS, 
Each user/device is given unique credentials for stronger security and management

slides.title: 4. WPA3
slides.body:
Introduction
Introduced in 2018, WPA3 addresses the weaknesses of WPA2 and is the latest and most secure Wi-Fi security standard

slides.title: 4. WPA3
slides.body:
Key Points
SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals): replaces the PSK handshake to prevent offline dictionary attacks
 Forward Secrecy uses unique session keys, so past data stays safe even if the password is later compromised

Open Network Protection (OWE – Opportunistic Wireless Encryption): Encrypts traffic even on open (passwordless) Wi-Fi networks like those in cafes and airports
Simplified Device Onboarding: Wi-Fi Easy Connect simplifies device setup via QR code for IoT devices
